extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination of process (method) claims that involve laws of nature, natural phenomena, or natural correlations, applying the Mayo/Prometheus framework to determine subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: State all non-cumulative reasons in first Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if one or more claims are found deficient under 35 U.S.C. 101, examiners should identify all non-cumulative bases for rejection (including other statutory grounds) in the initial review/first Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall practical-application/integration test (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Process claims having a natural principle as a limiting element or step should be evaluated by determining whether the claim includes additional elements/steps or a combination of elements/steps that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that the natural principle is practically applied, and are sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim as a whole satisfies this inquiry the claim is directed to patent-eligible subject matter; if not, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 as non-statutory subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry 1 — Is the claimed invention a process?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the claimed invention directed to a process, defined as an act, or a series of acts or steps? If no, this analysis is not applicable (see product claim guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process claims are sometimes called method claims. If the claim is not a process, evaluate under other appropriate MPEP sections (e.g., product claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry 2 — Does the claim focus on a natural principle?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim focus on use of a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or naturally occurring relation or correlation (collectively referred to as a natural principle)? (Is the natural principle a limiting feature of the claim?)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A natural principle is the handiwork of nature and occurs without the hand of man (examples: disinfecting property of sunlight; relation between blood glucose and diabetes). If the natural principle is not a limitation of the claim, this natural-principle analysis is not required (but consider abstract-idea analysis per MPEP §2106).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry 3 — Practical application/integration and 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim include additional elements/steps or a combination of elements/steps that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that the natural principle is practically applied, and are sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself? (Is it more than a law of nature plus the general instruction to simply 'apply it'?)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional elements or steps must relate to the natural principle in a significant way to impose a meaningful limit on claim scope; a bare statement of a natural correlation or adding only insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., recording a diagnosis on a chart) is insufficient. The claim must not effectively monopolize the natural principle or cover every substantial practical application of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — determine what applicant invented and broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the entire specification and claims to determine what applicant believes he or she invented. Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claims when read in light of the specification and from the view of one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim analysis begins by identifying and evaluating each claim limitation and then considering the claim as a whole. It is improper to dissect a claimed invention into discrete elements and then evaluate the elements in isolation. Use the same interpretation to evaluate compliance with statutory requirements (see MPEP §§2111, 2173 et seq.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration requirement — at least one additional element must practically apply the natural principle
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be at least one additional element or step that applies, relies on or uses the natural principle so that the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself; not every recited element must integrate the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements or steps that do not integrate the natural principle and are merely appended to it are not sufficient; the additional steps must meaningfully relate to the principle (e.g., change how it is implemented or confine it to a particular practical application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements or steps that are mere extra-solution activity unrelated to the correlation or principle (e.g., recording a diagnosis on a chart) do not make the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that merely adds routine administrative or data-recording steps to a natural correlation will fail Inquiry 3 because those steps do not integrate the natural principle into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding preemption — additional elements must meaningfully limit scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional elements or steps must narrow the scope of the claim such that others are not foreclosed from using the natural principle for future innovation; the claim must not cover every substantial practical application of the natural principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements that are well-understood, purely conventional, routine, or that merely limit field-of-use are insufficient. A claim that adds something that confines its reach to particular patent-eligible applications (e.g., a new drug) may be eligible even if the natural principle is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionality — well-understood, routine, conventional steps add nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps that amount to instructions that are well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by those in the field add nothing specific to the natural principle that would render it patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A showing that the steps are not routine, well-known, or conventional could be persuasive for eligibility; conversely, merely reciting conventional activity will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-Transformation (M-or-T) factors are relevant but not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The weighing factors used previously (including the Machine-or-Transformation test) are useful tools for assisting in the evaluation, but satisfying the M-or-T factors does not ensure eligibility if those features do not integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A particular machine or transformation recited in more than general terms may help show integration, but merely reciting a machine generically or a tangential transformation (e.g., only a change in position) may not. The machine/transformation should be described so as to show how it implements the natural principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims covering known and unknown uses or performable without apparatus are suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers known and unknown uses of a natural principle and can be performed through any existing or future-devised machinery, or even without any apparatus, would lack features that are sufficient for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such broad claims risk preempting the natural principle; eligibility favors claims with limiting, specific, practicable implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: A particular machine/transformation described in detail may show integration
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular machine or transformation recited in more than general terms may be sufficient to limit the application to a particular implementation such that the claim does not cover every substantial practical application of a natural principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing details of machine parts or how a transformation implements the natural principle (e.g., how parts of an internal combustion engine apply combustion to produce energy) helps show integration; nominal or incidental use of a machine does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal or tangential machine/transformation references do not show integration
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine or transformation that is merely nominally, insignificantly, or tangentially related to the steps or elements (for example, data gathering or data storage) would not show that these additional features integrate the natural principle into the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: using a computer as a counterweight rather than as a processing device; transformations involving only changes of position or location rather than changes in state or thing are insufficient to show integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of machine-or-transformation indicates likely disembodied claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete absence of a machine-or-transformation in a claim signals the likelihood that the claim is directed to a natural principle and has not been instantiated (e.g., is disembodied or can be performed entirely in one’s mind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of any machinery or transformation often suggests the claim merely recites an abstract or natural principle without concrete application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere statement of a general concept monopolizes the principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere statement of a general concept (natural principle) would effectively monopolize that concept/principle and would be insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with a tangible implementation recited with specificity: observable and verifiable steps or concrete machine details can provide the specificity needed so that not all substantial applications are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a rejection — required explanatory elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 for failing Inquiry 3, identify the natural principle, identify that the claim is effectively directed to the natural principle itself, and explain the reason(s) that the additional claim features or combination of features fail to integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention or fail to be sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an analysis of how the claim passes Inquiries 1 and 2 but fails Inquiry 3, and explain why the additional steps are insufficient (e.g., they are routine, conventional, generic, or merely appending extra-solution activity). The guidance includes a sample rejection template and a sample claim analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating applicant response — permissible amendments and arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper response to a rejection should add or amend steps/features that integrate the natural principle into the process (by practically applying or making use of the principle) and are sufficient to limit the application of the natural principle to more than the principle itself plus generalized application steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is also proper for the applicant to present persuasive arguments that the additional steps add something significantly more than merely describing the natural principle, or to show that steps are not routine, well-known, or conventional. Examples of both eligible and ineligible hypothetical claims may be used to demonstrate sufficiency or insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is distinct from patentability (other statutory requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is deemed eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101 is not necessarily patentable; it must also comply with other statutory and non-statutory considerations for patentability such as utility, double patenting, novelty (35 U.S.C. 102), obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103), and written description/definiteness (35 U.S.C. 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner analyses under 101 should not conflate eligibility with other patentability conditions; follow other MPEP sections as appropriate for those determinations.
